profile.behavior: Walks and stalks on the ground, probing soil and vegetation for insects; males sing from exposed perches and defend breeding territories with postures and flight displays. Often forms loose flocks outside the breeding season.
field_marks: Bright yellow throat and underparts crossed by a bold black V
Heavily streaked brown-and-black back and rounded wings
Striped crown with a yellow eyebrow and pale moustachial line
Long, straight, spear-shaped gray bill and dark brown eye
Long pale pinkish-gray legs with sturdy toes
Short barred brown tail with conspicuous white outer feathers
profile.habitat: Native grasslands, prairies, pastures, hayfields, wet meadows, agricultural fields, savannas, and other open grassy areas; nests on the ground in dense vegetation.

findings: The primary specimen is clearly identifiable as an Eastern Meadowlark: the bright yellow throat and underparts, bold black breast V, white moustachial stripe, striped crown, streaked brown-and-black upperparts, short barred tail with white outer feathers, long pointed bill, and long pale legs agree with the references and direct sources.

Overall proportions are credible for the species. The bill, dark eye, folded wing, tail, legs, anisodactyl feet, detached spread-wing study, and detached head study are coherent and free of material malformation. Minor stylization does not compromise identification.

There is exactly one primary bird with one head, one beak, two legs, one tail, and a normal lateral wing arrangement; the far wing is naturally occluded. The detached wing and head are unambiguously supplementary studies rather than attached or duplicate anatomy.
Every visible identification, measurement, habitat, behavior, and field-mark line matches the proposed wording and verified facts. The common name, scientific name, and family are correctly spelled.
The published ranges are correct: length 19–26 cm (7.5–10.2 in), wingspan 35–40 cm (13.8–15.8 in), and weight 90–150 g (3.2–5.3 oz).

The body-length ruler is internally consistent: 19 cm is at the bottom, 26 cm at the top, values increase upward, units and endpoints match the printed range, and it contains exactly four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks. The separate body-length label agrees, and “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE” prevents it from implying printed-bird scale.
The plate is legible, balanced, and visually organized; the primary specimen, supplementary studies, ruler, text, and palette remain clearly separated.
